new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is stated at the phrase level: the final syllable of a phrase is stressed, and that syllable is always heavy, where Bow defines heavy as containing a full (+Low) vowel rather than by CVC/CVV; the same page says the vowel in word-final pre-pausal position must be +Low. No word-level stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated in the footnote; the main text notes that in word-final pre-pausal position the syllable must be heavy (full vowel), which is the correlate of the phrase-final stress. Bow's 'heavy' is full versus reduced vowel, not syllable shape.
new_statements.identity_note: Bow 1997 (p. 1) reports that a 1996 SIL sociolinguistic survey found no distinctive dialects of Moloko, only village-level accent differences with full intercomprehension; her sketch is based on two speakers, one from Mbidémé (foot of Moloko Mountain) and one from the Ftak clan raised in Gayak Assideo. Works 2 and 3 are the same document (the 2004 SIL Cameroon version of Friesen & Mamalis, The Moloko verb phrase), and work 1 is its 2008 SIL EWP revision, so the four listed entries are really two distinct works.

Bow's 1999 evidence consists of citation (pre-pausal) forms, which cannot distinguish word-final from utterance-final stress; the later and fuller descriptions by Friesen & Mamalis (2004 p.10 fn.30, 2008 p.9 fn.29) and Friesen (2017 pp.38-39) explicitl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bow (1999) states a word-level rule: primary stress always on the word's final syllable; adding a suffix moves the stress onto the suffix (new final syllable) and the root's former final vowel changes ([+Low] full vowel only in the stressed, pre-pausal closed final syllable; [-Low]/schwa-grade in context). The same section ties the full-vowel alternation to citation (pre-pausal) vs. context form, i.e. the data shown are isolation forms. The language is also described as tonal (three register tones, lexical and grammatical tone).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (only 'primary stress' is named; no statement about secondary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in open syllables keep their underlying vowel height across morpheme and word boundaries (sec.3.4, ex.22), i.e. the stress-conditioned vowel alternation applies only to closed final syllables; no exceptions to final placement are given.

readall_conflicts: One wording-level disagreement. Bow 1999 (M.A. thesis, sec.3.4 p.22) writes that 'Primary stress in Moloko always falls on the final syllable in a word' and that a suffix 'shifts the stress', i.e. a word-domain fixed: final syllable rule, whereas the catalog (Friesen 2017 pp.38-39: 'the final syllable before a pause is stressed'), the statement held by the project from Bow 1997 (p.5 fn.5: 'stress falls on the final syllable in a phrase') and both versions of Friesen & Mamalis, The Moloko verb phrase (2004 p.10 fn.30; 2008 p.9 fn.29: 'The final syllable in an utterance is stressed') put the stress at the end of the phrase/utterance and tie it to the pre-pausal full-vowel requirement. All sources agree on FINAL position and on the diagnostic (stressed final syllable takes a full vowel, [a]-grade, vs schwa-grade in context); they differ only on whether the domain is the word or the utterance. Bow's 1999 examples are citation forms (words before pause), which do not discriminate; the three later, fuller descriptions restrict stress to utterance-final position, so the catalog's PHRASAL coding stands, with Bow 1999 noted as a word-level wording of the same observation. All sources also agree the language is tonal (3 surface / 2 underlying tones, lexical and grammatical tone).
